definition: Salutation means a greeting, especially one that opens a letter.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word salutation. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know salutation should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Every letter in the tin box opens with the same salutation — 'Dear little brother' — even after fifty years.
A nod falls far short of a salutation — the smallest acknowledgment there is: wordless, over in half a second, with none of the composed formality a salutation carries.
A greeting goes further than a nod — friendly words exchanged in passing — but it stops short of a salutation, the composed, formal opening that letters and ceremonies require.

Hello is the greeting word at its plainest — a single word that works anywhere, from a hallway to a phone call. A salutation is the composed, calibrated version: the formal opening a letter or a ceremony performs. Every salutation greets; hello would be underdressed where one is required.

A welcome is a greeting that also opens the door — it receives someone into a place or a group, and it cares about their arrival. A salutation opens a text or an occasion instead: the formal address before the substance. You give guests a welcome; you write readers a salutation.

Her predecessor phoned from retirement to reassure her.

Salutation is the exact word for what that desk checks, because a salutation is a greeting, especially one that opens a letter — the formal handshake a document performs before it says anything.
A hello is any greeting at all; a salutation is the composed, calibrated one, and its closing twin is the valediction, the formal goodbye.

The summer intern's first job at the law firm was digitizing a century of correspondence, one drawer per week.
She soon stopped reading the letters for their contents and started reading them for their openings.
The oldest, from 1908, began 'My dear and honored colleague'; by the 1950s the standard salutation had shrunk to 'Dear Mr.

Hale'; the last paper folder, from 2003, opened with a bare 'Hi all.' Nothing else about the letters changed half so much — the same complaints, the same billing disputes, the same requests for delay.
A century of business had kept its substance and rewritten only its manners, one opening line at a time.
